title: Where heaven and earth collide
caption: The Milky Way over La Silla Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at La Silla Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Observatory domes sit beneath a sky shimmering with stars at ESO's La Silla Observatory, high in Chile's Atacama Desert. A dense, bright band runs almost vertically across the frame, mottled by dark pockets of dust that block the light of stars behind them.

Every star here belongs to our own galaxy, the Milky Way, which holds billions of stars in two very different structures. A roughly spherical halo, made mostly of older stars, appears as the scattering of stars across the whole sky. A thin disc of younger stars, gas and dust forms the bright band.

Toward the top center of the band lies a bright concentration, the central region of the galaxy. There, astronomers have measured stars moving far faster than anywhere else in the Milky Way. They take this as evidence for a supermassive black hole of some four million solar masses. It cannot be seen directly, but its enormous gravity shows in the motions of nearby stars.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph credited to ESO/B. Tafreshi. The source does not publish camera, exposure or color-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the Milky Way's band may appear brighter and more detailed here than to an observer on site.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: ESO says the domes at La Silla hold some of the world's most advanced astronomical instruments, set here beneath the very sky they are built to study. The photograph is credited to B. Tafreshi of twanight.org.
alt: Observatory domes beneath a star-filled sky, with a bright, dust-mottled band of the Milky Way running almost vertically and brightest near the top center.
